note: Built incrementally from each case's verified extract; powers the merged Table of Authorities. Keyed by Indian Kanoon doc-id; each authority lists the cases that cited it and how it was treated.

15267.name: M.P. Electricity Board v. Harsh Wood Products

cited_by.proposition: No notice/opportunity required before disconnecting supply on a prima facie finding of theft; not violative of Articles 14 or 20(1) or natural justice.

755547.name: M.U. Sinai v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: A removal-of-difficulties power may only round off angularities and cannot alter a statute's basic structure or essential provisions (para 47).

335276.name: Maharana Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Income Tax Tribunal, Ahmedabad

cited_by.proposition: The Government's subjective satisfaction that a difficulty has arisen is not conclusive and remains open to judicial scrutiny.

1057604.name: Agricultural Market Committee v. Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: The Legislature must enunciate policy and principles before delegating subsidiary legislative power.
The seven principles governing express or implied ouster of civil-court jurisdiction under a special statute.

156242701.name: Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: Narrowed Dhulabhai's Principle (1): only non-compliance with fundamental statutory provisions or fundamental judicial procedure defeats the finality of a special tribunal's order.

1155660.name: Unique Butyle Tube Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Financial Corporation

cited_by.proposition: The principles of casus omissus and reading a statute as a whole to avoid an absurd or anomalous result.

22637242.name: M/s. Paliwal Alloys (Pvt) Limited v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd

cited_by.proposition: Held that theft of electricity under Section 135 is also unauthorised use of electricity for which assessment under Section 126 is contemplated. The sixth proviso to Section 135(1A) refers to ‘assessed amount’, confirming concurrent assessment. Right of appeal under Section 127 is available even in theft cases. Applied as controlling precedent of this Court.

181377341.name: M/s Radha Krishna Cold Storage v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: A Division Bench observed that mere non-mention or incorrect mention of relevant provisions does not vitiate the assessment order; the order is referable to Section 126 and appeal lies under Section 127 even where the order purports to be under Section 135.

The order under challenge is an assessment order (which can be passed only under Section 126) even if wrongly cited under Section 135; mere non-mention or incorrect mention of the relevant provision does not vitiate it. Substantive statutory rights of appeal cannot be taken away by any provision framed in subordinate rules.

897981.name: Ashok Kumar and Others v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that unauthorised use as defined in Explanation (b) of Section 126 covers acts/omissions that constitute an offence under Section 135. The assessing officer must record its conclusion and give an opportunity of hearing before concluding that a person is indulging in unauthorised use.

Unauthorised use of electricity as defined in explanation (b) of Section 126 covers acts that constitute offences under Section 135. No person can be indicted and held guilty of unauthorised use unless given an opportunity of hearing before conclusion of assessment. Natural justice and procedural fairness require opportunity of hearing even in theft cases.

759180.name: Chairman, West Bengal State Electricity Board and Others v. Syed Mukbul Hossain and Others

cited_by.proposition: Apex Court noticed the right of appeal under Section 127 even in a case of theft of electricity, confirming that assessment procedures apply in theft cases.
Affirmed the right of appeal under Section 127 in cases of theft of electricity, confirming that assessment procedures must afford statutory appeal rights and due process.

864296.name: Tinsukhia Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam & Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that the provision of a statute must be construed as to make it effective and operative; courts should lean against any construction which tends to reduce a statute to futility. Applied to interpret Sections 126 and 135 in a harmonious manner so both are workable.

46574637.name: Varun Kumar Yadav v. State of U.P. and Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that the 24-hour requirement for lodging FIR under Section 135(1-A), Electricity Act, 2003, is not merely directory but is mandatory and imperative. Applied the principle that ‘once a particular thing is directed to be done in a particular manner, anything done otherwise will be void and illegal.’ Against this judgment, a Special Leave Petition was filed before the Apex Court (SLP (Crl.) Diary No. 74474 of 2025), with notices issued on 23.1.2026.

102224597.name: Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. State of U.P. and 4 Others
102224597.cite: Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 265 of 2023, dated 6.2.2013

cited_by.proposition: Held that Section 135(1-A)'s 24-hour requirement is only directory, carrying no consequences for breach. Distinguished and found to be per incuriam because it failed to consider Section 57 of the Electricity Act and Clause 8.2 of the UP Electricity Supply Code 2005, both of which prescribe substantive consequences for non-compliance with the timeline.

19775419.name: Dr. Arun Kumar v. Nagar Nigam, Bareilly

cited_by.proposition: Established the foundational principle that ‘once a particular thing is directed to be done in a particular manner, anything done otherwise will be void and illegal.’ Applied to establish that the 24-hour requirement is substantive and compliance therewith is mandatory.

1652054.name: Malwa Industries Ltd. Vs. Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Held that captive-user ownership may be aggregated and need not be 26% per individual member; equity shares with voting rights constitute “ownership”; and supply from a CGP to a shareholder-sister concern, without a license, is permissible subject to open-access regulations. Applied to establish that M/s. Kherani Paper Mills Ltd., holding 37.86% in the CGP owner, is a captive user.

1726045.name: Nalwa Steel & Power Ltd. Vs. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held that open-access regulations apply only when open access (grid) is availed of; if no grid access is used and a dedicated line serves a captive user or nearby consumer, the generating company cannot be forced to route power through the grid; and dedicated lines connecting a CGP to a load centre (including a single consumer) are permissible without a license. Relied on to support the Tribunal’s discussion of transmission rights and the distinction between dedicated-line supply and open-access supply.

43074463.name: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill

cited_by.proposition: Drew the Section 126 (unauthorised use, civil) / Section 135 (theft, criminal, mens rea) distinction. Held not to assist the licensee: it did not decide the determination or method of assessing civil liability in theft cases.

76510513.name: Kadodara Power Pvt. Ltd. and Others v. Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission and Another

cited_by.proposition: Interpreted Rule 3(1)(a) proviso to hold that a SPV is equivalent to an Association of Persons and therefore subject to the proportionality test (51% ÷ 26% = 1.96% per 1% shareholding, ±10%). The judgment applied this holding to deny full captive status to SPVs without meeting the proportionality requirement. Treated as foundational by respondents and cited in subsequent Tribunal appeals (Prism Cement, JSW Steel, Sai Wardha).

Referred to only as it figures within Dakshin Gujarat: the Supreme Court affirmed Kadodara’s reasoning that proportionality of consumption is assessed against the qualifying 51% requirement and not against 100% of generation. Not independently applied by this Court.

27707757.name: Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Co. Ltd. v. Shri J.P. Saboo, Urla Industries Association Ltd. & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held (paras 34–35) that a Distribution Licensee or State Transmission Utility cannot determine captive-plant status; only the State Commission, in exercise of its regulatory powers under Section 86(1)(f), is the appropriate authority to determine captive status. This principle is foundational to the adjudication function.

42991347.name: Prism Cement Limited v. Madhya Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held (para 9.6, 10.1) that the twin requirements under Rule 3(1)(a)(i) and (ii) must be verified together, on an annual basis at the end of the financial year, with the status determined fresh each year. Rule 3 recognises that a power plant can be a CGP in one year but lose that status in a subsequent year if the conditions are not met. Verification at year-end is the correct timing for both ownership and consumption.

1619801.name: Uma Nath Pandey & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.

cited_by.proposition: Laid down the settled principle that no person can be made a judge in his own cause; this is fundamental to natural justice and impartiality in quasi-judicial proceedings.

29616041.name: Salasar Steel and Power Ltd v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission and Others

cited_by.proposition: Held that verification of captive status must be done on an aggregate (not individual or component-wise) basis. The aggregate shareholding and consumption are the operative criteria; individual non-compliance does not nullify the collective’s status if the thresholds are met.

1393954.name: Jitendra Kumar Singh v. State of U.P.

cited_by.proposition: Held that in reading a judgment, isolated observations cannot be treated as precedent dehors the facts and circumstances in which the observation was made. The ratio decidendi—the principle upon which the case was decided—is binding, not every observation or dictum.

1145726.name: Union of India v. Dhanwanti Devi

cited_by.proposition: Held that it is the ratio decidendi—the principle on which a case is decided—that is binding, not every observation. A decision is an authority for what it actually decides; what is of essence is the ratio, not every observation found therein.

1613962.name: State of Orissa v. Mohd. Illiyas

cited_by.proposition: Reiterated that a decision is a precedent on its own facts, and reliance on a decision without looking into its factual background is impermissible. The ratio, not every observation, is binding.

170697.name: Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal & Anr.

cited_by.proposition: Laid down that a Court, out of judicial propriety, ought not to have decided an issue which was not presented before it for adjudication. Deciding an issue not on the agenda violates judicial propriety.

55040.name: V.K. Majotra v. Union of India & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held that a judicial body should not decide an issue that was not presented before it for adjudication; doing so violates principles of proper procedure and natural justice.

150450225.name: Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Solar Semiconductor Power Co.(India) (P) Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Held that a Commission, being a creature of statute, cannot assume powers not conferred on it. Under the guise of inherent power, a Commission cannot exercise a power whose procedure is specifically provided under the Act.

121318562.name: Sesa Sterlite Ltd. v. Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Recognized CSS as a key component for maintaining the efficacy of the open-access system and as a major source of revenue for the Distribution Licensee.

630814.name: Panchi Devi v. State of Rajasthan

cited_by.proposition: Held that a delegated legislation is ordinarily prospective in nature; a right or liability created for the first time cannot be given retrospective effect unless the parent Act permits.

Held that if the Act does not confer power on the delegatee to make regulations with retrospective effect, the delegatee cannot do so, as it is well settled that absence of such power prevents retrospective operation of delegated legislation.

33840213.name: State of Rajasthan v. Basant Agrotech (India) Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Confirmed that a delegated authority exercising delegated powers can only exercise those powers specifically conferred; in the absence of conferment, a delegated authority has no power to issue a notification with retrospective effect.

103037015.name: K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh & Another

cited_by.proposition: Held that introduction of a new criterion after a process is completed amounts to changing the rules of the game after the game was played, which is clearly impermissible. This principle applies to regulatory procedures affecting settled transactions.

Established that an 'association of persons' must be one in which two or more persons join in a common purpose or action to produce income, profits or gains. An association is a combination of individuals not constituting a partnership under law.

1691505.name: CIT v. Buldana Distt. Main Cloth Importer Group

cited_by.proposition: Held that where the business was carried on as one unit by consent of all parties, and profits were ascertained and distributed according to capital contributed by each member, the entity constituted an 'association of persons'.

1267220.name: Ramanlal Bhailal Patel v. State of Gujarat

cited_by.proposition: Held that the ordinary, natural meaning of 'person' in law refers to any entity having rights and duties; 'association of persons' is an unincorporated entity that may be recognized by law. Once an association is incorporated, it becomes a company.

1659123.name: State of Punjab v. Kailash Nath

cited_by.proposition: Held that a proviso to a provision only embraces the field covered by the main provision; it carves out an exception to the main provision to which it has been enacted as a proviso and to no other.

506242.name: Ram Narain Sons Ltd. v. Asst. CST

cited_by.proposition: Laid down the cardinal rule of interpretation that a proviso to a particular provision only embraces the field covered by the main provision. It carves out an exception to the main provision and to no other.

109918.name: Union of India v. Sanjay Kumar Jain

cited_by.proposition: Held that the normal function of a proviso is to except something from the enactment or to qualify something enacted; a proviso does not normally travel beyond the provision to which it is a proviso. A proviso must be read with the principal matter to which it stands as a proviso.

1273462.name: Vemareddy Kumaraswamy Reddy v. State of A.P.

cited_by.proposition: Held that where the words of a statute are clear and unambiguous, there is no scope for the court to innovate or amend the statutory provisions. Judges should not proclaim themselves law-makers; there is a line between adjudication and legislation.

1772349.name: Mohd. Shahabuddin v. State of Bihar

cited_by.proposition: Held that courts cannot read anything into a plain and unambiguous statutory provision. The language of the statute is determinative of legislative intent. Where the legislature prescribes a condition at one place but not another, the omission is intentional, not inadvertent.

187431175.name: Adani Transmission Limited v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Held that a previous judgment of a co-ordinate Bench can be declared per incuriam if it was given in ignorance of a statute or rule having statutory force, or in ignorance of a binding precedent. A judgment per incuriam does not form a binding precedent.

16382121.name: Delhi Municipal Corporation v. Gurunam Kaur

cited_by.proposition: Set out the test for determining whether a judgment is per incuriam: a decision given in ignorance of a prior decision or of a statutory provision is rendered per incuriam and may not bind a subsequent co-ordinate Bench.

607688.name: M/s. Consolidated Coffee Ltd. v. The Agricultural Income-Tax Officer, Madikeri & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Held that Delayed Payment Charges (DPC) are in the nature of compensatory charges, not tariff income, and must be distinguished from other revenue sources.

Affirmed that the aggregate 26% ownership and 51% consumption thresholds are the operative criteria; once met by the collective, individual non-compliance does not strip the collective of captive status.

186863738.name: M/s Sai Wardha Power Co. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Anr.
186863738.cite: Appeal No. 316 of 2013 (referenced in Salasar Steel judgment)

cited_by.proposition: Referenced for the holding that proportionality of consumption is measured against the qualifying 51% requirement, not against 100% of total generation. Also applied the concept of weighted-average shareholding (which is now under challenge in pending appeals A. No. 340 & 341 of 2018).

1375346.name: A.N. Sehgal v. Raje Ram Sheoran

cited_by.proposition: Held that a proviso must be considered with relation to the principal matter to which it stands as a proviso. A proviso carves out an exception to the main provision.

27395.name: Kerala State Housing Board v. Ramapriya Hotels (P) Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Held that a proviso normally does not travel beyond the provision to which it is a proviso. It carves out an exception to the main provision and to no other.

880618.name: Ansal Properties & Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana

cited_by.proposition: Referred to in context of not reading words into a plain statutory provision; courts cannot add to the language of a statute.

395434.name: PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
395434.cite: Constitution Bench judgment (not reported with year/series in the text)

cited_by.proposition: Statutory provisions and regulations, as part of the regulatory framework, override existing contracts between regulated entities.

1848972.name: M.K. Shah Engineers and Contractors v. State of M.P.
1848972.cite: Supreme Court judgment (not fully cited in text)

cited_by.proposition: No party can be permitted to take advantage of its own wrong; if one party delays or procrastinates, procedural prerequisites are deemed waived and the defaulting party cannot invoke them.

655432.name: Kusheshwar Prasad Singh v. State of Bihar and others
655432.cite: Supreme Court judgment (not fully cited in text)

cited_by.proposition: Authorities cannot take undue advantage of their own default in failure to act in accordance with law within reasonable time; no authority can profit from its own wrongdoing.

15924357.name: The Chairman, State Bank of India and another v. M.J. James
15924357.cite: Supreme Court judgment (not fully cited in text)

cited_by.proposition: Courts must consciously examine whether a party chose to sit idle over a matter and awakened only to gain advantage; prejudice to the other party must be factored even when laches exist.

574042.name: Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Co. Ltd. v. District Board, Bhojpur
574042.cite: Supreme Court judgment (not fully cited in text)

cited_by.proposition: A party cannot take undue advantage of its own wrong.

1469962.name: Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd. and others
1469962.cite: Supreme Court judgment (not fully cited in text)

cited_by.proposition: Respondents cannot take advantage of their own wrong; such conduct amounts to taking unfair advantage.

cited_by.treatment: Cited (as foundational framework, but subordinated to IBC)
cited_by.proposition: Sections 56, 173, 174, 175 establish the framework for recovery of electricity dues, disconnection of supply for non-payment, and authorize the State Commission to frame regulations (such as the Electricity Supply Code) for recovery.
Sections 14, 33, 35, 50, 53, 238 establish the comprehensive regime for insolvency resolution and liquidation; Section 238 grants absolute overriding effect to the Code over all other laws.

109520577.name: Section 53, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — Waterfall Mechanism

cited_by.proposition: Establishes the priority order for distribution of liquidation proceeds: (1) costs of IRP/liquidation; (2) secured creditors and workmen dues (capped); (3) employees; (4) unsecured financial creditors and workmen; (5) government dues; (6) remaining debts; (7) surplus to shareholders.

160269658.name: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board and others
160269658.cite: 2023 SCC Online SC 663 : (2023) 9 S.C.R. 637; Civil Appeal No. 2109–2110 of 2004

cited_by.proposition: Electricity utilities can create a statutory charge to recover arrears from subsequent transferees through subordinate legislation or statutory conditions of supply, grounded in the public interest of protecting utility infrastructure.

5808278.name: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited and Others

cited_by.proposition: An electricity supply company that participates in an IBC proceeding is treated as a secured creditor under the waterfall mechanism (Section 53) and cannot demand payment from a resolution applicant or new owner; its dues must be satisfied through the liquidation process according to priority.

183986005.name: Tata Power Western Odisha Distribution Limited (TPWODL) & Anr. v. Jagannath Sponge Private Limited
183986005.cite: Company Appeal (AT) No. 5556 of 2023 (Supreme Court judgment)

cited_by.proposition: A power company cannot insist on payment of arrears (which must be paid under the waterfall mechanism) for grant of an electricity connection to a successful resolution applicant; however, the applicant must comply with other requirements for connection.

181931435.name: M/s Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank

cited_by.proposition: Section 238 of the IBC mandates that the provisions of the Code shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other law; the non-obstante clause is ‘in the widest terms possible’ to preclude any right under any other law from impeding the Code.

1992542.name: Duncans Industries Ltd. v. A.J. Agrochem

cited_by.proposition: Section 16G of the Tea Act, 1953 (requiring Central Government consent for winding up) is overridden by the IBC, establishing that even substantive requirements of sectoral statutes yield to the IBC.

42502475.name: CIT v. Monnet Ispat and Energy Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: The IBC’s overriding effect under Section 238 is absolute and applies to tax and revenue statutes.

73508068.name: K. Kishan v. Vijay Nirman Company Private Limited

cited_by.proposition: The IBC overrides the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; the IBC’s comprehensive framework takes precedence over other procedural statutes.
